title: The Double Push Explained: How Inline Speed Skaters Get More From Every Stride
thumbnail_text: Two pushes, one stride, more speed

scenes.heading: The Double Push Explained
scenes.sub: More speed from every stride, for the same effort
scenes.narration: By the end of this guide you will know what the double push is, and how to learn it step by step. You will also know where it belongs on the track and what it asks of your skates. Ask experienced inline speed skaters when they finally got fast, and many will point to one moment. It was the day the double push clicked. It is the stroke that lets marathon and track skaters hold high speeds for long stretches while looking almost relaxed. It is also one of the most misunderstood moves in the sport. From the outside it just looks like normal skating done smoothly. It is a feel first skill. So the aim here is a clear picture in your head and a sensible way to build it.

scenes.heading: What the double push is
bullets: Classic stroke: one push per leg
Double push: two pushes, one stroke
Set down inside your body line
Push inward, then roll and push out
scenes.narration: Start with a classic stroke. You set the skate down under you, roll onto an edge, and push out to the side. Then you bring the leg back and repeat on the other side. That is one push per leg. The double push adds a second push at the start of the same stroke. Instead of setting the skate straight down, you place it slightly to the inside of your body, on an inside edge. You push inward briefly. Then you roll the skate across to the outside edge and deliver the familiar outward push. Two pushes, one leg, one stroke.

scenes.heading: Single push vs double push
scenes.narration: Here is the difference seen from above. The single push travels one way, straight out from the centre line. The double push first curves inward on an inside edge, then rolls across and pushes outward. In a single push stroke, the moment you set the skate down gives you no drive. It is just a landing. In a double push, that landing becomes an active inward push. So you make force across a longer part of each stroke. More of your stride does useful work. That is why skaters can hold a higher cruising speed without a higher heart rate, once the move feels natural.

scenes.heading: The inside edge is the secret
bullets: Set the skate inside your track
Load the inside edge, push inward
Relax the ankle and roll across
Two pushes, one connected sweep
scenes.narration: The heart of the double push is the inside edge push. When you set the skate down slightly inside your body line and push inward, you load the inside edge of your wheels. You use it to send force toward your centre. This feels strange at first, because most skaters are taught to keep the set down right under the body. Learning to trust that inside edge is the biggest hurdle. It is why the move takes weeks, not days. Once the inside push is spent, relax the ankle. Let the skate roll from the inside edge, through flat, onto the outside edge. That roll is smooth, not a flick. Then deliver the main outward push. The two pushes should feel like one connected sweep.

scenes.heading: The edge roll, front view
scenes.narration: This front view shows what the wheel does across one stroke. It starts on the inside edge, where you push inward. It rolls across through flat. Then it reaches the outside edge, where you push outward. The inward push loads the inside edge. The outward push loads the outside edge. Notice that the roll in the middle is not a separate move. It is the bridge that joins the two pushes together. If you rush it, the stroke breaks into two separate efforts. If you let the ankle relax, it flows.

scenes.heading: Straights, not corners
bullets: Double push on the straights
Crossovers through the corners
Load the inside edge out of a bend
Long road straights reward it most
scenes.narration: The double push is a straightaway stroke. In a corner you are crossing over, and the crossover already keeps both legs working. Trying to double push through a bend just breaks your rhythm. The skill is to link the two. Finish your last straight stroke cleanly, drop into the crossover, and come out of the corner straight into a connected double push. That exit is where most skaters lose speed. The first stroke out of the corner is rushed and never loads the inside edge. On a 200 metre track the straights are short, so you may fit only two or three full strokes. On the road and in a marathon, the straights run for hundreds of metres. There, the double push becomes the stroke you live in. In a pack, it keeps your feet closer to your centre line, so you can sit close behind another skater.

scenes.heading: What it asks of your setup
bullets: A stiff, light race frame
Wheels matched to weight and surface
Clean bearings carry the glide
One drop of oil after a clean
scenes.narration: The double push loads both edges of the wheel hard, again and again. So your equipment has to keep up. A flexy or badly mounted frame robs you of the crisp edge changes the stroke depends on. A stiff race frame sends your inside and outside pushes straight into the wheels instead of soaking them up. Wheels matter just as much. A wheel that is too hard for you will slip during the inside push. Match firmness to your body weight and the smoothness of your usual surface. Finally, bearings decide how much of your speed survives between strokes. Keep them clean, and give them a single drop of bearing oil after a clean. A dry or gritty bearing scrubs off exactly the glide the double push is built to protect.

scenes.heading: Learn it in three stages
scenes.narration: Do not try a full double push at speed on day one. Build it in layers. Stage one. Skate slowly and set each skate clearly inside your body line, then push out as normal. This teaches your body to accept a set down that is not right underneath you. Spend a whole session on that. Stage two. At a gentle roll, set the skate inside, press onto the inside edge, and feel it push you toward your centre. Then roll across and push out. It will feel clumsy, and that is fine. Stage three. Only when the inward push and the roll feel connected, add tempo and blend it into full speed skating. Slow and correct comes first. Speed comes last.

scenes.heading: The one foot glide check
bullets: Glide on one skate at walking pace
Tip from inside edge to outside
Feel the wheel steer under you
Five minutes at every session
scenes.narration: Here is a useful check between stages. It is the one foot glide drill. Roll on one skate at walking pace. Tip it from the inside edge to the outside edge and back. Feel the wheel change direction under you each time. If you cannot steer a single skate with its edges while gliding, you are not ready to load those edges inside a stroke. Do five minutes of this at the start of every session. It builds the ankle control the double push depends on. Rushing straight to race pace usually bakes in a rushed, broken stroke that is hard to unlearn.

scenes.heading: Common mistakes
bullets: Hip wiggle with no inside edge
A jerky stamp between pushes
Setting the skate too far inside
Shoulders and hips swinging
scenes.narration: The most common error is faking it. Many skaters wiggle their hips and believe they are double pushing, but they never load the inside edge. If you do not feel a clear inward push against that edge, you are just swaying. Slow down and hunt for that pressure. The second mistake is a jerky change between the two pushes. The roll must come from a relaxing ankle, not a sudden stamp. The third is setting the skate too far inside, so you cannot recover your balance. Keep the inside set down modest until your edges catch up. The fourth hides in the upper body. Keep the torso quiet and low. Swing the arms straight forward and back, not across the body. Filmed from behind, a good double push shows the skates weaving while the head and shoulders track almost straight.

scenes.heading: Quick answers
bullets: Learn a clean single push first
Expect weeks, then months
Works on big wheels and triskates
Taller setups need extra slow sessions
scenes.narration: Do you need the double push to enjoy inline speed skating? No. Plenty of skaters stay quick with a clean single push. Learn that first, then add the double push when your edges are reliable. How long does it take? Most skaters need several weeks of patient, slow practice before it feels connected, and months before it is automatic at race pace. Progress comes in sudden jumps, so do not lose heart. Does it work on bigger wheels and three wheel frames? Yes. Taller wheels roll further per stroke and reward a smooth double push even more. But a taller setup tips onto its edges a little less quickly. So give yourself extra slow sessions to find the inside edge.

scenes.heading: Turn the landing into a push
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: The double push is not a trick. It is a more complete way of using each stroke. Set the skate slightly inside your body, push against the inside edge, roll smoothly across to the outside edge, and finish with the usual outward push. You turn the dead landing of ordinary skating into real drive. Learn it slowly, keep it for the straights, and add tempo only once it feels connected. The full guide is on the LiveLica blog, with every diagram and the frequently asked questions. The link is in the description.
